steps.prompt: AI writes the code in seconds. So what are you paid for?
steps.sub: This is the round that lands the offer — and the one AI can't sit for you. By the end you'll run the operator's loop: write a tight spec, delegate to the agent, REVIEW its output like a senior, and correct it under interview pressure. You direct AI. You don't fear it.

steps.prompt: In the AI era, when the agent can type faster than you ever could — what is the engineer's actual value?

options.t: Directing + verifying the agent — judgment, decomposition, and review. You own the spec and the gate, not the keystrokes.
Memorising more syntax than the AI knows.

steps.why: Code generation is now cheap and fast. What stays scarce — and what every interview is really testing — is judgment: breaking a vague problem into a clear spec, delegating it, then catching what the agent got subtly wrong. You become the senior reviewer of an infinitely fast junior. That shift IS the job.
hints: If the agent does the typing, what's left that only a human does well?
Think: spec, delegate, review, correct — which of those can't be outsourced?

steps.prompt: The operator's loop: spec → delegate → review → correct.
steps.sub: Tap each card. This is the TrigunAI signature — run it on every problem.

cards.b: State the goal, constraints, edge cases, and the complexity target BEFORE the agent writes anything. A vague prompt gets vague code.
Hand the well-scoped task to the agent. Let it draft fast — you don't write the boilerplate.
Read the output like a senior: is the complexity right? does it handle empty/null/huge inputs? did it over-engineer?
Redirect precisely: 'this is O(n²), use a hash set' — not 'try again.' Then re-review. Loop until it's actually right.

steps.prompt: The agent's solution runs and passes the happy-path example. Why is a senior still not done?
steps.sub: This is the moment juniors ship and seniors keep going.

options.t: They're done — it passed the test, that's the whole job.
Passing the happy path proves nothing about complexity, edge cases, or whether it used the right approach. Those are exactly what break in production and in follow-up questions.
They should rewrite it from scratch by hand to be safe.

steps.why: 'Runs on the example' is the floor. Before trusting the agent you verify three things: the complexity (is it secretly O(n²)?), the edge cases (empty input, one element, duplicates, overflow, nulls), and the approach (did it over-engineer a 5-pattern monster for a 3-line problem?). That review is the value you add over the raw agent output.
hints: What does 'passes one example' actually guarantee? Almost nothing.
Three checks: complexity, edge cases, right approach.

steps.prompt: Sort each line: is it good DIRECTING, or a junior anti-pattern?
steps.sub: Tap an item, then a bin. How you talk to the agent decides what you get back.

items.t: "Make it O(n) with a hash map; handle the empty-array case."
"Add an edge-case test for duplicates, then re-run."
Copy-pasting the output without reading it.
"State the time + space complexity of your solution."
Accepting a 5-pattern design for a problem that needs none.

hints: Good directing is SPECIFIC — names the target, the constraint, the edge case.
Trusting blindly or asking vaguely is where it goes wrong.

steps.prompt: Put the operator's loop in order for one interview problem.
steps.sub: Run this every time and you'll look senior even when the agent does the typing.
chips: Write a tight spec: goal, constraints, edge cases, complexity target
Delegate the draft to the agent
Review: check complexity, edge cases, and approach
Correct with a precise redirect, then re-review until right
hints: You can't delegate cleanly until you've written the spec.
Review comes before correction; correction loops back to review.

steps.prompt: Run a live round: 'find the longest substring with no repeating characters.' Command the agent.
steps.sub: The interviewer is watching HOW you direct and verify, not whether you can type it.
steps.goal: Get a correct, O(n), edge-case-safe solution — by directing the agent.

turns.situation: You've got the problem. The agent is ready.
options: Spec it: 'sliding window, O(n) target, handle empty string and all-same'
turns.log: 📝 Spec → sliding window, O(n), edge: empty + all-same.

turns.situation: The agent returns a solution using two nested loops. It passes 'abcabcbb'.
turns.q: It passed the example. Your call?
options: Flag it: that's O(n²) — redirect to a sliding window with a seen-set
Ask for more comments and ship
turns.log: 🔍 Caught O(n²) → redirect to sliding window.

turns.situation: The agent rewrites it as a proper O(n) sliding window.
turns.q: Before you approve, what do you demand?
options: Test the edge cases: empty string, single char, all identical chars
turns.log: 🛠️ Edge cases requested → empty + single + all-same all pass.

turns.situation: Complexity is O(n), edge cases pass, approach is clean.
turns.q: Final step in front of the interviewer?
options: Own it: explain WHY it's O(n) and the tradeoff, as if you authored it
Say 'the AI did it' and shrug
Loop forever asking for more changes
turns.log: ✅ Owned the solution + reasoning. Offer-grade answer.

hints: Spec, catch the cost, demand edge cases, then own the reasoning.
The interviewer hires the judgment, so you must explain it as your own.

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check.

statements.t: If the agent's code passes the example, you can trust it and move on.
statements.why: No — happy-path pass is the floor. You still verify complexity, edge cases, and that it didn't over-engineer before trusting it.

statements.t: A precise redirect ('use a hash set, it's O(n)') beats a vague one ('try again').
statements.why: Right — specific direction gets the fix on the first try; 'try again' often gets you a different wrong answer. Directing is a skill.

statements.t: In the AI era you no longer need to understand complexity or design — the agent handles it.
statements.why: No — you can only REVIEW and CORRECT what you understand. Your DSA + design knowledge is exactly what lets you catch the agent's mistakes. The agent raises the bar, it doesn't remove it.

statements.t: You should be able to explain the agent's final solution as if you wrote it yourself.
statements.why: Yes — in the interview you OWN the answer. 'The AI did it' fails you; explaining the why, the complexity, and the tradeoffs is what gets the offer.

hints: Trust is earned by verification, not by a single passing test.
Understanding is what makes review possible — it doesn't go away.

steps.sub: Not graded. This is your operator's pledge for the job hunt.
